title: How to approach an investment or capacity case
description: The first question to ask in an investment or capacity case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Should the client build a new plant, add capacity or make a big investment? Here is how to think it through.
body:
The first question to ask

Is demand real, and can existing capacity be squeezed?

How to build your structure

  • Need (is demand real and lasting, squeeze existing capacity first)
  • Economics (upfront and running cost, extra margin, payback, price effect if rivals add capacity)
  • Alternatives (outsource, lease, subcontract)
  • Execution (time to build, skills, risks)

The trap most people fall into

Approving capex before fixing bottlenecks.

For the full tree, with every branch, read the investment decision framework.

Two prompts to try

Should a car maker build its own battery plant?

Show a model structure
  • Need: Our battery demand and supply security; Prices and lead times from suppliers
  • Make vs buy economics: Plant cost vs buying, per kWh; Payback and NPV
  • Risks: Technology changing fast; Can we run a plant at scale?
  • Alternatives: Joint venture, long-term supply contracts; Buying a stake in a supplier

Where to start: Make vs buy cost per kWh over the life of the plant.

The trap: Ignoring that battery technology may change before the plant pays back.

Should a supermarket open dark stores for 15-minute delivery?

Show a model structure
  • Demand: How many orders per dark store per day; Density: orders within a 15-minute radius
  • Economics per order: Basket size, delivery fee; Picking, delivery, rent per order
  • Cannibalisation: Orders taken from our own stores and online; Net new profit
  • Competition and operations: Rapid-delivery rivals burning cash; Can we staff and stock it?

Where to start: Economics per order: rapid delivery usually loses money on every order at low volume.

The trap: Assuming every order is new and not taken from our own stores.
outro: Small things like this add up. Try it in your next practice case and notice how it changes the conversation. Practise this case type in the free casebook: every case has a worked answer.
